parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the first law of thermodynamics. Identify the meaning of any symbols that you use.

markscheme_points.text: change in internal energy = work done +
increase in internal energy = work done

hints: Hint 1: Think about conservation of energy for a gas - its stored internal energy can only change if energy crosses the system boundary in one of two ways.

Hint 2: Recall the two transfer routes are heating and mechanical working, and be ready to write $\Delta U = q + w$ with clear definitions of $q$ as heat supplied to the system and $w$ as work done on the system.
parts.proper_answer: The increase in internal energy of a system is equal to the sum of the thermal energy supplied to the system and the work done on the system: $\Delta U = q + w$, where $\Delta U$ is change in internal energy, $q$ is thermal energy (heat) supplied to system, $w$ is work done on system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Cannot Be Created - Only Transferred**
Think of the gas as an energy store. Its internal energy $U$ is the sum of the random kinetic energies of all its molecules. For an ideal gas this depends only on temperature. To make $U$ larger you must put energy in from outside, and there are only two ways to do that.

Step 2: **Writing the First Law With Symbols**
Heating puts energy in as thermal energy $q$, and compressing or expanding transfers energy as work $w$. Using $\Delta U$ for the change in internal energy:
$$\Delta U = q + w$$
Here $q$ is positive when thermal energy is supplied TO the gas, and $w$ is positive when work is done ON the gas. So the law says: change in internal energy = thermal energy supplied + work done on gas.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
Complete Table 3.1 for the changes A to B and B to C by placing two ticks (✓) in each row.

Table 3.1

| change | change in internal energy | | | work done on gas | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | decrease | no change | increase | negative | zero | positive |
| A to B | | | | | | |
| B to C | | | | | | |

markscheme_points.text: AB change in internal energy: decrease
AB work done on gas: positive
BC change in internal energy: increase
BC work done on gas: zero

hints: Hint 1: For an ideal gas, internal energy follows temperature only, so use $pV = nRT$ to decide whether $T$ rises or falls when $p$ or $V$ changes.
Hint 2: For A to B, look at what happens to volume at constant low pressure and link this to temperature and to whether the gas is compressed or expanded.
Hint 3: For B to C, look at what happens to pressure at constant volume and link this to temperature.
Hint 4: Remember work done on the gas is positive for compression, negative for expansion, and zero when volume does not change.
parts.proper_answer: A to B: change in internal energy = decrease, work done on gas = positive. B to C: change in internal energy = increase, work done on gas = zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A to B - Compression At Low Pressure**
From Fig. 3.1, A to B is a horizontal line to the left at constant pressure. Volume decreases, so the gas is compressed and work is done ON the gas, so $w$ is positive. From the ideal gas law:
$$pV = nRT$$
With $p$ constant and $V$ decreasing, $T$ must decrease. For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so internal energy decreases.

Step 2: **B to C - Heating At Constant Volume**
B to C is a vertical line upwards. Volume is constant, so:
$$w = p\Delta V = 0$$
No work is done on or by the gas. Pressure increases at constant $V$, so from $pV = nRT$, $T$ must increase. Therefore the internal energy increases. That gives two ticks in each row: A to B (decrease, positive) and B to C (increase, zero).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Use the first law of thermodynamics to describe and explain the energy transfers associated with one complete cycle ABCDA.

markscheme_points.text: more work done by gas in CD than is done on gas in AB or (no work done on gas in BC and DA so)
(overall) change in internal energy is zero
(must be an overall) input of thermal energy

hints: Hint 1: Start by comparing the two horizontal stages - expansion CD at high pressure and compression AB at low pressure - which involves the larger $p\Delta V$ work?
Hint 2: Think about what happens to internal energy after one full loop when the gas returns to exactly the same $p$ and $V$ at A, and hence the same temperature.
Hint 3: Combine your net work and net $\Delta U$ conclusions using $\Delta U = q + w$ to decide whether heat must overall enter or leave the gas.
parts.proper_answer: More work is done by the gas in expansion CD than is done on the gas in compression AB, with zero work in BC and DA, so there is net work done by the gas. Over a complete cycle $\Delta U = 0$. By the first law there must be a net input of thermal energy equal to the net work done by the gas.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Net Work Is Done BY the Gas**
Work is only done in the constant-pressure stages because $w = p\Delta V$. CD is an expansion at high pressure, so a large amount of work is done BY the gas ($w$ negative). AB is a compression at low pressure, so a smaller amount of work is done ON the gas ($w$ positive). BC and DA are constant volume, so $w = 0$. Overall more work is done by the gas than on the gas, so the net work is done by the gas. This is the area enclosed by rectangle ABCDA.

Step 2: **Internal Energy Returns To Start**
Point A is the same state at the start and end of the cycle, so $p$, $V$ and therefore $T$ are the same. Since $U$ depends only on $T$ for an ideal gas:
$$\Delta U_{cycle} = 0$$

Step 3: **First Law Demands Net Heat Input**
Apply $\Delta U = q + w$ to the whole cycle:
$$0 = q_{net} + w_{net}$$
Since $w_{net}$ is negative (net work by gas), $q_{net}$ must be positive. In words, thermal energy must be supplied to the gas overall to keep the internal energy unchanged while the gas does net external work.
